new_statements.second_reader_evidence: PRIMARY QUOTE CHECK. File (18 pp., image-only scan, PDFCreator/Ghostscript; extracted text yields 3 chars). I rendered PDF p. 2 at 300 dpi, inspected the page image directly and ran tesseract on it. The page carries the running head "66 Journal of West African Languages XXIX.1 (2002)" and, under the heading "1.2 TONE", reads exactly: "Denya has two level tones, high [ ´ ] and low [ ` ], and two contour tones, rising [ ˇ ] and falling [ ˆ ]; and a downstep high [ ꜜ ]." The bracketed diacritics on the page are acute, grave, caron/wedge, circumflex and a down-arrow; the report's transcription is faithful. Locator "p. 66, §1.2 TONE (PDF page 2)" is correct. The section is the whole of the tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Denya is described as a register-tone language (H, L, rising, falling, downstepped H); none of the three accessible descriptions makes any statement about word stress, its position, or its absence. No rule for stress placement can be stated from an opened source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement to have exceptions).
new_statements.domain_note: Mbuagbaw 2002 is a noun-class morphology article by the language's principal describer (CABTAL) with a one-page phonological overview; the tone statement is lexical/word-level (examples are nouns with prefix tones). Bakume 2005 is a comparative D.E.A. thesis whose Denya sketch is of the Takamanda (reference) dialect. Neither is the full phonology (Mbuagbaw 1996/1999), which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Mbuagbaw 2002 treats Denya as a whole (four dialects: Takamanda, Basho, Betieku, Bajwa; data from a CABTAL language committee). Bakume 2005's phonology sketch is explicitly of the Takamanda reference dialect. Glottolog 5.3 lists deny1238 with alternative names Anyang/Anyah/Nyang/Takamanda/Obonya and no dialect-level glottocodes on the page fetched sources. Abangma 1992 calls the language 'Ekoid Bantu'; Mbuagbaw 2002 places it in the Nyang sub-group of Southern Bantoid.

sources.note: §1 'Overview of vowels, consonants, and tone' (pp. 65-66): 7 vowels, consonant chart, and §1.2 TONE: two level tones (H, L), two contour tones (rising, falling) and a downstep high. Stress/accent is not mentioned anywhere in the 18 pages (scan had no text layer; scanned at 300 dpi and grep-checked).

sources.note: Bibliographic only; the LDH page lists Seguin 1998, Bakume 2005 and Mbuagbaw 1999 as the Denya descriptions.

sources.citation: Bakume Nkongho Ojong, Magdaline. 2005. The proto-reconstructions of the Nyang languages. D.E.A. dissertation, University of Yaounde I (supervisor Ngessimo Mutaka). 162 pp.
sources.note: Ch. 2 'A brief phonology and noun class system of the Nyang languages' gives a Denya sketch (Takamanda dialect: 20 consonants, 7 vowels, syllable patterns, 2.2.4 Tones, thesis p. 21 = PDF p. 32): 'The Denya language has two tones underlyingly: the High and Low tones. All the other forms are derived just like Kenyang.' No stress statement for Denya; the only occurrence of 'stress' (p. 9, lit. review) describes Tyhurst's 1984 Kenyang phonology report as analysing 'suprasegmental features of stress, length, and tone'.

sources.citation: Abangma, Samson Negbo. 1992. Empty categories in Denya. PhD thesis, University College London (ProQuest 10609199). 276 pp.
sources.note: Syntax (GB) thesis; no phonology chapter. Only p. 11 'Tone marking: Only high tone is marked. The unmarked is low tone.' Nothing on stress (the word occurs only in the non-technical sense). Note 1 refers to Abangma 1987: 1-3 for details about the language.
